name: Verteporfin hair

lead: Verteporfin is a prescription drug used with a red laser to treat abnormal blood vessels in the eye. Online hair communities follow it as a possible way to regrow follicles in scarred or donor areas and to heal hair transplant surgery with less visible scarring.

Lab studies suggest it can block YAP/TEAD signalling, which affects how fibroblasts respond to injury and form scars. Evidence for hair is limited to mouse studies and a few surgeon-reported cases discussed on forums.

paras: Its approved use is an intravenous, light-activated eye therapy. Hair use is experimental and discussed mainly online, with no standard routine or controlled human trials.

The label warns of photosensitivity, extravasation, vision changes and anaphylaxis for the approved eye use. Safety for scalp use has not been studied in controlled trials. Hair use is not an approved indication.

angle.text: Forum posters discuss verteporfin as a way to regrow follicles in transplant scars and to heal cosmetic surgery with less visible scarring, which some see as a route to repeated transplants. It is an eye-disease drug with lab research on the Hippo pathway. The appearance use rests on mouse studies and a few clinician-reported cases.

lead: Verteporfin (brand name Visudyne) is a light-activated drug approved for photodynamic therapy of abnormal blood vessels in the eye, for example in wet age-related macular degeneration, pathologic myopia and presumed ocular histoplasmosis.[1][2] Separately, laboratory research has examined it as an inhibitor of the YAP-TEAD interaction in the Hippo signalling pathway.[3]

In looksmaxxing communities, verteporfin is discussed as an experimental way to reduce scarring and to regenerate hair follicles in scarred or donor areas after hair transplant surgery, a use some posters describe as a route to repeated transplants. This use is not an approved indication, and the human evidence for hair is limited to a few clinician-reported cases discussed online rather than controlled trials.

paras: Visudyne is indicated for predominantly classic subfoveal choroidal neovascularization due to age-related macular degeneration, pathologic myopia or presumed ocular histoplasmosis.[1] It is a two-stage treatment: the drug is infused and then activated by non-thermal red light, producing reactive oxygen species that damage the endothelium of abnormal vessels and occlude them.[1] Wikipedia also notes off-label use for central serous retinopathy.[2]
Grokipedia reports the original FDA approval date as April 12, 2000, with development by QLT Inc. and marketing by Novartis; that source is AI-generated.[4]

The label lists injection-site reactions and visual disturbances as the most common reactions (over 10 percent), and warns of extravasation, photosensitivity (patients are advised to avoid direct sunlight or bright indoor light for several days after infusion), decreased vision after treatment and anaphylactic reactions; porphyria is a contraindication.[1] In rats given roughly 40 times the human exposure, the label reports increased anophthalmia or microphthalmia.[1]
These data relate to the approved intravenous, light-activated eye treatment. No safety data from controlled studies of verteporfin injected into or applied to the scalp are available.

sections.h: Use in hair and scarring research
paras: Preclinical work has linked the YAP/TAZ and TEAD pathway to fibrosis and scar formation. A 2021 Science paper reported that preventing Engrailed-1 activation in fibroblasts, including by treating mouse wounds with verteporfin, allowed regenerative wound healing without a scar.[5] Studies in other tissues have implicated YAP/TAZ in kidney fibrosis and described YAP-TEAD disruption by verteporfin in cancer models.[3][6]
Wikipedia states that verteporfin is experimentally applied to reduce scarring in hair transplantation, citing the American Hair Loss Society, and gives no study details.[2]

No controlled clinical trial of verteporfin for hair growth or hair-transplant scarring was found. The human trials of verteporfin concern its approved ophthalmic use, including the TAP trials in macular degeneration and comparisons with ranibizumab.[7][8][9] Registered trials also exist in glioblastoma and breast cancer photodynamic therapy.[10][11]

Threads on looksmax.org present verteporfin as a possible route to "infinite" hair transplants and scarless surgery, citing a hair transplant surgeon's update on small case series, in which hair was reported to regrow in scarred transplant areas after nine months. Another thread summarises laboratory findings on YAP/TAZ and argues the drug might reduce fibrosis in transplants, cosmetic surgery and acne scarring. Other users in these threads raise cost concerns, with one reply stating a price of about 100 dollars per square centimetre.
Community protocol posts also exist and describe self-experimentation with research-grade material; this wiki does not reproduce such instructions.

lore.intro: Verteporfin is discussed on looksmax.org mainly as a hair-transplant adjunct and scar-reduction compound, based on laboratory papers and a clinician's informal case reports.

claims.claim: Verteporfin can regrow follicles in transplant scars and enable "infinite" hair transplants.
Verteporfin enables scarless healing after cosmetic surgery and may remove acne scars.
The compound is too expensive for most users.

timeline.event: Visudyne approved by the FDA for choroidal neovascularization (per Grokipedia).[4]
Genes & Development paper reports verteporfin disrupting the TEAD-YAP complex in a cancer model.[3]
Science paper links Engrailed-1 inhibition, including verteporfin, to scarless wound regeneration in mice.[5]
